core_principles.text: Start in a standing position and then take a step with one foot.
Position one foot in front and one foot behind the torso, similar to a split stance.
Keep the feet about hip-width apart during the setup.
Ensure the distance between the front foot and back foot is a length that is greater than a walking stride.
The torso should be straight and the abdominals should be tight.
The scapula should be retracted and depressed with the eyes looking forward.
The toes and knees of both legs should be pointing forward.
The back heel should be off the ground.
The distance between the front and back foot should be a length that is greater than a walking stride.
While keeping the torso straight and abdominals tight, lower the hips until both knees are bent at about a 90-degree angle, if possible.
Make sure the front knee is directly above the ankle and not over the toe.
Push through the front heel to return to the starting position while contracting the glutes, quadriceps, and calves.
Once in the appropriate starting position, the hips should move down and up in a straight line.

common_mistakes.text: Quite often, the lunge is plagued from the start due to a stride length that is too short.
Even a slight turn of the lead foot or lead knee inward during a forward lunge can occur.
The back foot is often externally rotated for stability compensation.
Beginners tend to lean too far forward during the eccentric phase of the exercise.
To compensate for balance and strength challenges, the torso can lean forward during the downward phase.

specific_findings.text: At the lowest point of the downward movement, the hip, knee, and ankle joints should be no less than 90 degrees.
While keeping the torso straight and abdominals tight, lower the hips until both knees are bent at about a 90-degree angle, if possible.

consequences.text: If the feet are too close together, the downward movement results in an increased amount of stress on the knee joint, specifically the patellar tendon.
Even a slight turn of the lead foot or lead knee inward during a forward lunge can increase the torque stress of the knee joint of the front leg, potentially leading to increased knee pain.
Rotating the back knee or foot outward during a forward lunge increases torque stress in the knee joint.
Leaning too far forward during the eccentric phase can increase the shear force at the knee joint, increasing the risk of injury or pain.
Lunges performed without optimal technique can create unnecessary joint stress that can limit performance, exacerbate pre-existing injuries, and potentially cause pain.

core_principles.text: The lunge does not have to be a full movement to be effective, as even a small range of motion will activate the muscles used, challenge balance, and incorporate functionality.
Once the initial position is achieved, the lunge can be performed effectively without movement of the feet until the repetitions are completed.
Elevating the front leg just a few inches decreases stress on the front leg, reducing the difficulty of the lunge.
Using a chair for support and reduced range of motion allows the glute of the front leg to sit on the chair during the lower phase before returning to the starting position.
Performing side lunges places more mechanical stress on the muscles of the hip joints, specifically the glutes and hamstrings.
Incorporating an unstable surface under the front leg forces stabilizer muscles to activate more and prime movers to work harder.
Holding weight with straight arms overhead, in front, or to the sides of the body increases the lever length, making the lunge more difficult.
Performing split squat jumps from a split stance without a forward step can be used to increase power.

consequences.text: Elevating the front leg decreases stress on the front leg.
Using an unstable surface under the front leg forces the stabilizer muscles to activate more and prime movers to work harder to execute the movement.
Holding weight further away from the moving joints increases the lever length, which increases the difficulty of the exercise.
Performing side lunges increases mechanical stress on the muscles of the hip joints, including the glutes and hamstrings.
